How to generate a RESTful API request on Cisco Nexus Dashboard?
Version: 6.3.1
IP: 192.120.45.67
API name: get information of an interface
Parameter_fabricName: Network1
Parameter_nodeId: 12
Parameter_podId: 10
Parameter_interfaceType: Ethernet
Parameter_infoType: Speed

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Send a GET request to retrieve specified information for an interface from a network telemetry API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The URL endpoint to send the GET request to. This should include the base path without query parameters, e.g., 'https://{ip}/sedgeapi/v1/cisco-nir/api/api/telemetry/flowrules/interfaceInfo'.

params.description: The query parameters for the request.

fabricName.description: The name of the fabric to limit nodes pertaining to.

nodeId.description: The node identifier to limit results pertaining to.

podId.description: The pod identifier to limit results pertaining to.

interfaceType.description: The type of the interface to limit results pertaining to.

infoType.description: The type of information requested for the interface.

Below is a quick‑start guide that shows **how** you would build and fire off the request you described against a Cisco Nexus Dashboard instance. I’ll cover the three most common ways people do this today – a raw `curl` command, a short Python snippet (using the helper function you supplied), and a note on how you’d do it inside the Dashboard UI itself. --- ## 1. Build the URL & Query String | Parameter | Value | Notes | |-----------|-------|-------| | Base URL | `https://192.120.45.67/sedgeapi/v1/cisco-nir/api/api/telemetry/flowrules/interfaceInfo` | This is the “endpoint” part – no query string here. | | Query Params | `fabricName=Network1`
`nodeId=12`
`podId=10`
`interfaceType=Ethernet`
`infoType=Speed` | These come straight from your spec. | Putting it together (URL‑encoded): ``` https://192.120.45.67/sedgeapi/v1/cisco-nir/api/api/telemetry/flowrules/interfaceInfo?fabricName=Network1&nodeId=12&podId=10&interfaceType=Ethernet&infoType=Speed ``` > **Tip:** If you’re typing this into a browser or a tool that auto‑encodes spaces, make sure you keep the exact casing (`Ethernet`, not `ethernet`) because the API is case‑sensitive. --- ## 2. Fire It Off ### A. Using `curl` ```bash curl -k \ -u : \ # Basic Auth – replace with real creds "https://192.120.45.67/sedgeapi/v1/cisco-nir/api/api/telemetry/flowrules/interfaceInfo?fabricName=Network1&nodeId=12&podId=10&interfaceType=Ethernet&infoType=Speed" ``` * `-k` skips certificate verification (use only if you’re OK with self‑signed certs). * Replace `` / `` with your actual credentials or use a bearer token header instead. ### B. Using the Helper Function (Python) If you want to embed this in a script or notebook, you can call the function you gave me: ```python from functions import requests_get response = requests_get( url="https://192.120.45.67/sedgeapi/v1/cisco-nir/api/api/telemetry/flowrules/interfaceInfo", params={ "fabricName": "Network1", "nodeId": 12, "podId": 10, "interfaceType": "Ethernet", "infoType": "Speed" } ) print(response) # whatever the function returns (likely JSON) ``` > **Note:** The function will handle the HTTP GET under the hood. Make sure you’ve authenticated first (e.g., by setting a session cookie or passing an Authorization header). ### C. Inside the Nexus Dashboard UI 1. Log in to the Dashboard web console. 2. Navigate to **Developer → REST API Explorer** (or similar – the exact menu may vary by version). 3. Choose **GET** as the method. 4. Paste the full URL (including query string) into the “Request URL” field. 5. Click **Send Request**. 6. Inspect the returned JSON in the UI’s response pane. --- ## 3. Quick Checklist | ✅ | Item | |----|------| | ✅ | Verify you’re hitting the correct API version (`v1`). | | ✅ | Confirm the fabric name (`Network1`) exists on the controller. | | ✅ | Ensure the node ID (`12`) and pod ID (`10`) are valid for that fabric. | | ✅ | Double‑check the interface type spelling (`Ethernet`). | | ✅ | Use HTTPS and supply proper auth (Basic or Bearer). | | ✅ | If you hit a 401/403, check that your account has the *Telemetry Viewer* role (or equivalent). | --- ## 4. What Happens Next? Once you hit the endpoint, you should receive a JSON payload that looks something like this (example output): ```json { "fabricName": "Network1", "nodeId": 12, "podId": 10, "interfaceType": "Ethernet", "infoType": "Speed", "data": { "portSpeed": "100Gbps", "currentRate": "80Gbps", "maxRate": "100Gbps" } } ``` You can then parse this JSON in your downstream logic (Python `json.loads()`, JavaScript `JSON.parse()`, etc.) and feed it into Grafana dashboards, alerting systems, or any other tooling you use. --- ### TL;DR ```bash curl -k -u user:pass "https://192.120.45.67/sedgeapi/v1/cisco-nir/api/api/telemetry/flowrules/interfaceInfo?fabricName=Network1&nodeId=12&podId=10&interfaceType=Ethernet&infoType=Speed" ``` Or, in Python: ```python response = requests_get( url="https://192.120.45.67/sedgeapi/v1/cisco-nir/api/api/telemetry/flowrules/interfaceInfo", params={"fabricName":"Network1","nodeId":12,"podId":10,"interfaceType":"Ethernet","infoType":"Speed"} ) ``` That’s all you need to generate the RESTful request you asked about!
